transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Janine Herbst.
Stocks open sharply lower this morning
as the Commerce Department reported stronger economic growth
during the summer and early fall.
NPR's Scott Horsley reports the Dow and Nasdaq
are down more than 1,000 points in early trading.
The U.S. economy grew faster in July, August, and September
than initially reported.
Revised figures from the Commerce Department
show GDP expanded at an annual rate of 4.3 percent
in the third quarter.
The upward revision was largely the result
of stronger investment and consumer spending.
Demand sparked by booming investment
in artificial intelligence is also fueling inflation.
Prices in October were up 3.8 percent from a year ago,
according to the Commerce Department's yardstick,
which is closely watched by the Federal Reserve.
That's a bigger annual increase than the previous month.
The Fed's widely expected to respond by raising interest
rates at its next meeting in two weeks.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.
Newly reinstalled Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang
goes before a congressional panel next week
amid bipartisan concern.
He stepped down from the CEO role after reports of affairs,
including one with a suspected Chinese spy.
NPR's Maham Javed says lawmakers
are also considering new legislation.
There's concern about whether China has direct
or indirect access to these chips.
So they're looking at three bills with bipartisan support
that would restrict this movement of chips to China.
One would track where the chips go to try and prevent smuggling.
Another would tighten restrictions on chip-making
equipment from ending up in China.
And a third would limit sales of advanced chips to China.
NPR's Maham Javed reporting.
The U.S. Army detonation of a stockpile
of nearly five tons of unstable explosives containing lead
is set to get underway in Iowa.
It has residents taping their windows and doors
and some leaving the area worried
about the possibility of a toxic cloud
that could hurt humans, livestock and crops.
Colombian security forces have ended a 17-hour standoff
by storming a supermarket and freeing about 20 people
held hostage by gunmen.
John Otis has more.
Several explosions were heard early Wednesday morning
just before police and army troops entered the supermarket
where armed men were holding the hostages.
President Abelardo de la Esprella described the kidnappers
as common criminals who took refuge inside the supermarket
after they failed to rob cash from an armored truck.
Speaking at a news conference, the president said one
of the gunmen was killed after he refused
to release the hostages.
The kidnappings occurred as Colombians marked the 10th
anniversary of a peace treaty that disarmed the country's
largest guerrilla group.
For NPR News, I'm John Otis in Bogota.
On Wall Street, the Dow was down 643 points,
the Nasdaq down 718.
This is NPR News.
For those who can't afford a ticket to the Super Bowl
and don't especially relish watching the event on TV,
there's a third option.
And here's Chloe Veltman reports IMAX theaters
will be screening the big game for the first time
ever in February.
ESPN's telecast of the Super Bowl on Valentine's Day
next year will be screened across hundreds of IMAX
locations across the United States.
Football fans in some international markets,
such as Australia, New Zealand, and Brazil,
will be able to watch the action on IMAX's massive screens,
too.
The four-hour-long presentation will
include a telecast of the main game,
the halftime show headlined by hip-hop artist Jay-Z,
and pre-game and post-game coverage.
The Walt Disney Company, which is organizing the event
alongside IMAX ESPN and the NFL,
calls the upcoming screening a milestone in cinema
and the largest live event in IMAX history.
IMAX theater tickets for Super Bowl 61
are expected to go on sale in January.
Chloe Veltman, NPR News.
Online safety laws are now tougher in Australia.
The country's parliament has passed the Digital Duty
of Care Act that could lead to multi-billion dollar
fines for big technology companies that
failed to prevent foreseeable online harms.
But the US says that law could lead
to censorship of lawful speech.
The act puts the onus on those big tech companies, which
are largely from the US, to address online harm
and sets minimum safety standards for online services,
including games, apps, and AI bots.
Similar laws were passed in the European Union and the UK.
Again on Wall Street, the Dow was down 605 points,
NASDAQ down 723, S&P 500 down 145.
You're listening to NPR News.
Want to hear this podcast without sponsor breaks?
Amazon Prime members can listen to NPR News
now, sponsor free through Amazon Music.
Or you can also support NPR's vital journalism
and get NPR+ at plus.npr.org.
That's plus.npr.org.

topics.text: US economy grew 4.3% in third quarter per revised Commerce Department figures, stocks fall sharply
Inflation rose 3.8% in October, likely prompting Federal Reserve interest rate hike next meeting
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to testify before congressional panel amid bipartisan chip-smuggling concerns
Three bipartisan bills would restrict advanced chip sales and equipment flow to China
US Army to begin detonating nearly five tons of unstable lead-containing explosives in Iowa
Colombian forces storm supermarket, ending 17-hour hostage standoff; one gunman killed
IMAX theaters will screen Super Bowl 61 on Valentine's Day, with tickets going on sale in January
Australia passes Digital Duty of Care Act imposing fines on big tech over online harms; US objects
